propositions.evidence: we proposed a novel interface prototype, ParaLib, that helps programmers compare and select libraries at the level of concrete code examples
Distinct from these tools, ParaLib displays many code examples, with features to support comparison, not the process of searching, collecting, and cleaning information
We focus on four key dimensions identified in Vargas et al.'s need-finding study: fit for purpose, size, complexity, and usability
Key interface design choices were derived from the design implications of two theories of human concept learning: Variation Theory (VT) and Analogical Learning Theory (ALT)
ALT suggests that highlighting analogical concepts, i.e., functional correspondences, across all examples from all libraries will help the programmer appreciate—and see past—superficial differences
VT suggests that many varying examples shown in parallel may help programmers form more robust conceptualizations of the libraries' similarities and differences
highlighting analogical concepts... will help the programmer appreciate—and see past—superficial differences
a hierarchy of concepts... over which to compare the functionality of each library
rendering many concept-annotated code examples from different libraries side-by-side can help programmers develop a more comprehensive understanding
participants using ParaLib made more consistent, suitable library selections
the distribution of the number of examples from each library that contain code labeled with that concept
the distribution over the number of lines in each code example (top of Figure1③) is rendered for each library
selecting concepts at any level of the functional concept hierarchy allows users to toggle the highlighting of individual concepts...and filter the collection
Two additional buttons are intended to help users focus on functionalities they most care about and more easily see possible additional connections across libraries
We designed and implemented ParaLib as a technical probe and evaluated it in a within-subjects user study (N=20)
compared to participants using only online search, participants using ParaLib made more consistent, suitable library selections
participants made more consistent library selections when using ParaLib than when using online search
participants inspected 3 times more examples when using ParaLib than when using online search
participants wrote nearly three times longer responses when using ParaLib than when using online search in both domains
participants experienced significantly less mental demand, effort, hurry, and frustration when using ParaLib instead of online search
This could be attributed to the many concept-annotated code examples shown in ParaLib, through which participants could gather concrete details
participants also thought they had better performance when using ParaLib... these differences were all statistically significant
participants using online search made more divergent choices and became indecisive when comparing libraries along some dimensions
online search provided a less organized plethora of information, with less support for sensemaking and integration than ParaLib
16 of these 17 participants found ParaLib more useful than online search for comparing functionalities across multiple libraries

The hierarchy is currently designed by hand, in this case by the authors... Reaping the benefits of a ParaLib-like interface in a scalable way will require future investments in automatic or crowdsourced concept labeling
